response.text:
Tallec and Ollivier’s chrono initialization matches initial gate timescales to an anticipated dependency range, assuming roughly centered inputs and hidden states. For the convention h_t=z_t h_previous+(1−z_t)candidate, z is the retention gate: choose T uniformly over [T_min,T_max] and b_z=log(T−1), giving nominal z=1−1/T. The commonly quoted version is b_z∼log(U[1,T_max−1]), corresponding to T_min=2. This means logarithms of uniformly sampled values, not uniformly sampled logarithms. The sign reverses when z instead multiplies the candidate. [Original paper, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.11188)

Deterministic log-spaced τ∈[2,32] with b_z=logit(exp(−1/τ)) is a related variant, not the original prescription. Algebraically, it sets z=exp(−1/τ), so the isolated retention path decays as z^k=exp(−k/τ): τ is its exact discrete-time e-folding horizon. Original chrono uses the approximation T=1/(1−z); its exact e-folding horizon is −1/log(1−1/T), approximately T−1/2 for large T. Log-spacing assigns comparable numbers of units per multiplicative interval, emphasizing shorter horizons more than uniform-T sampling.

The paper motivates horizons using expected dependency lengths; it does not establish 2–32 as universally appropriate or require T_max to equal sequence length. That range is defensible as a tunable prior if retained, nonpadding histories contain useful dependencies over those interaction counts. Truncation limits accessible history; padding should not advance the recurrent state. These are nominal initialization horizons, not measured effective memory: input-dependent gates, candidate recurrence, nonlinearities and training change information retention and gradient propagation. A defensible claim is “chrono-inspired initialization with deterministic geometric horizons,” with the endpoints justified through training-history statistics and validation ablations.
